searchDocs.title: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
🛡️ Key Features​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security

searchDocs.title: Zero-Knowledge Email Encryption​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
searchDocs.content: Your privacy is now backed by industry-standard cryptography. Using AES-256 and Argon2id, your incoming emails are encrypted the moment they hit our gateway.  The "Three Words" Secret: We never store your decryption key or your secret words. When you download a message, your key is rebuilt from your three words and used only in transient memory for that request.Benefit: Even if our servers were compromised, your data remains indistinguishable from random noise.

searchDocs.title: The Route Listener (Smart Automation)​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
searchDocs.content: Stop the manual back-and-forth of whitelisting. The new Route Listener allows you to open a specific "airlock" for a set duration (30m, 1h, or 8h).  How it works: It catches the next incoming email, automatically whitelists the sender, and then snaps shut.Perfect for: Quick sign-ups and newsletter subscriptions without leaving your inbox exposed.

searchDocs.title: One-Click Data Portability​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
searchDocs.content: True privacy requires an exit strategy. You can now download your entire configuration — channel, routes, contacts, and permission settings — in a single, portable JSON file. Your setup belongs to you, not our database.

searchDocs.title: Instant Account Deactivation​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
searchDocs.content: We believe in the "Right to be Forgotten." If you choose to leave, our new one-click deactivation ensures all your records and configurations are purged from our infrastructure immediately.

searchDocs.title: 📱 Minor UI & UX Improvements​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
searchDocs.content: We’ve polished the interface to ensure your "Inbox Zen" follows you across all devices:  iOS Dark Mode Fix: Resolved a display issue where the Email Summary columns were unreadable in dark mode.Mobile Responsiveness: Fixed table overflow issues on mobile browsers; managing your routes on the go is now a seamless experience.Route Table Logic: Improved visibility for Subscription Route statuses and listener indicators.

searchDocs.title: 🔐 The Duotail Trust Guarantee​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Duotail v0.3.0: Total Sovereignty & Zero-Knowledge Security
searchDocs.content: Note on Encryption: Because Duotail is a zero-knowledge system, we do not have a "backdoor." If you lose your secret words, encrypted messages become permanently inaccessible. We prioritize your security over our convenience.  New to these features? Check out our updated Encryption Protocol Documentation or learn how to use the Route Listener.

searchDocs.title: What is a Contact?​
searchDocs.content: A Contact is a trusted sender assigned to a channel. Emails originating from a Contact bypass Route configurations to reach any address under that channel. For example, if angry.gazelle@example.com is a Contact for a_happy.rhino, their emails will always be delivered to a_happy.rhino@duotail.com, _sports, and _food regardless of specific route rules.

searchDocs.title: Contact Properties​
searchDocs.content: Each Contact object includes the following properties:  Contact Email: The external, real-world email address of your contact.Contact Name: A display name used to identify the contact (independent of their email address).Email to Send: The specific duotail.com address you should use as the Recipient field when composing an email to this contact.Route (Optional): A specific route you wish to designate as the "Sender" address for this contact.Notes (Optional): A field for any personal reminders or extra information regarding the contact.

searchDocs.title: Incoming Email Handling​
searchDocs.content: When our system detects an incoming email from a channel contact, it processes the message and delivers it to your inbox immediately.

searchDocs.title: Outgoing Email Handling​
searchDocs.content: When the system detects an outgoing email addressed to a channel contact, the following checks are performed before the message is delivered:  Sender Permission Check: The system verifies that the user has the necessary permissions to send emails from this account.Inbox Authentication: The system ensures that the sender's originating inbox matches the designated recipient email address for either the specific Channel or Route.

searchDocs.title: Sending to Several Contacts (Paid Plans)​
searchDocs.content: You can put any number of 2_ contact addresses in the To, Cc and Bcc fields of one email, up to 50 different addresses.  One email, every recipient: Each contact receives the same message from your masked channel address. Contacts in To and Cc can see each other and can reply all; contacts in Bcc stay hidden.Only contacts are kept: Any address that is not a 2_ address (for example a real address you also typed, or another Duotail address) is removed from the email we send.Missing contacts: If any 2_ address has no contact yet, the whole email waits in Send Pending on your dashboard. When you click Send, you are asked to create a contact for each missing address in turn. If you stop part way, the contacts you already created are kept and the email stays pending until you finish.Sending limit: Each recipient counts as one email toward your plan's monthly sending limit.History: The email appears as a single row on the History page, however many recipients it has.Too many recipients: An email with more than 50 different 2_ addresses is not sent.

searchDocs.title: Reply All on Received Emails​
searchDocs.content: When someone emails you and copies other people, your copy shows those other people under Duotail addresses that start with 3_ (or 4_ for very long addresses), for example ABC <3_abc_at_example.com@duotail.com>. Their names are kept, so you can still tell who is who.  If you click Reply All in your mail app, your reply comes back through Duotail and goes out to everyone from your masked address, so your real email address stays private.  Reply only: 3_ and 4_ addresses work only in a reply to the email they came from. You can't use them to start a new email.Non-contacts warning: When the email arrives at a channel's main address, the Email Summary lists any participants who aren't contacts of that channel. If you reply all, their replies to you are blocked until you add them as contacts.Large groups: If an email has more than 50 other participants, reply all is turned off for that email. It is still delivered to you, and you can still reply to the sender.

searchDocs.title: Alias Notice​
searchDocs.content: When you write to a contact through their 2_ address and the contact belongs to an alias channel, Duotail adds a short notice at the top of the email:    Anyone can choose the sender name of an alias channel, so the notice tells your contact not to rely on it. The notice is permanent: it stays in the conversation when people reply, and it is hidden when the email is printed. Emails from an identity channel don't get the notice.  The notice is also not added when your email is signed or encrypted, or when you send from a mailbox at an encrypted-mail provider such as Proton, because changing the content of those emails would break them.

searchDocs.title: What is a Channel?​
searchDocs.content: A Channel acts as an "umbrella" for all email addresses starting with its name. For example, owning the channel a_happy.rhino gives you ownership over any emails starting with a_happy.rhino, for example a_happy.rhino@duotail.com, a_happy.rhino_sports@duotail.com, and a_happy.rhino_food@duotail.com.  Channel and Inbox On our web page, channels are listed under Inboxes. An inbox and a channel are the same thing; "inbox" is simply the name the web page uses.

searchDocs.title: Channel Email​
searchDocs.content: A channel email is an address where the local part (the text before the @ symbol) matches the specific channel name. For example, the channel a_happy.rhino uses the email address a_happy.rhino@duotail.com as its channel email. On the Inboxes page, the channel email is shown in the Main Email column.

searchDocs.title: Security and Contact Managemen​
searchDocs.content: Channel emails operate on a whitelist-only basis; only senders included in the channel's contact list are permitted to send messages to that address. Additionally, when an outgoing email is sent via the channel, the recipient is automatically added to the contact list to ensure seamless future communication.

searchDocs.title: Channel Type​
searchDocs.content: There are two types of channel: alias channel and identity channel.

searchDocs.title: Alias Channel​
searchDocs.content: An Alias Channel is provided to all users who wish to utilize our services without verifying their legal identity. We believe everyone deserves an email address that isn't tied to their real-world persona. Consequently, every account includes at least one default alias channel, following the format: a_<your_username>@duotail.com.  All our alias channel starts with a prefix "a_". So, via the email address itself, the recipients of these emails should be able to tell if they from an anonymous sender. For example, a person received an email from a_harry.potter@duotail.com, he can tell the sender is A Harry Potter not The Harry Potter.  On our web page, an alias channel is marked with a theater icon     Because anyone can choose the sender name of an alias channel, an email you write to a contact's 2_ address from an alias channel carries a short notice at the top: Sent from an alias address. The sender name was chosen by the alias owner and may not match their real identity. The notice stays in the email and is hidden when the email is printed. See Alias Notice for details.

searchDocs.title: Identity Channel​
searchDocs.content: An Identity Channel is assigned to users whose real-world identities have been successfully verified. Unlike alias channels, an Identity Channel email address has no prefix (e.g., isacc.swordblessing@duotail.com). This serves as a "verified badge," signaling to recipients that the sender's identity is authentic and confirmed.  On our web page, an identity channel is marked with an id badge icon     note Identity channel name contains at least one dot. It's used to differentiate from our organization emails such as support@duotail.com

searchDocs.title: Channel Limits by Plan​
searchDocs.content: Plan	Alias channels	Identity channelsFree	The alias channel created when you register	Not available Basic	Up to 3, including the one created when you register	Up to 1  Every channel you have created counts toward the limit, whether or not it has been activated yet. Channels you already own are never removed, even if you have more than your plan allows; you just can't add new ones until you are under the limit.

searchDocs.title: What is an Email Summary?​
searchDocs.content: An Email Summary is a system-generated table inserted at the beginning of every incoming email, providing a concise overview of the message's original content. This summary is automatically removed when you reply, ensuring the external recipient never sees it.  We include the Email Summary for following key reasons:  Enhanced Visibility: Standard email headers are often insufficient—especially on mobile platforms—for quickly identifying key details.Transparency and Security: We believe users have the right to know what might be hidden within a message. The summary notifies you of "invisible" elements, such as whether the email contains tracking pixels or insecure links.One-Click Sovereignty: We provide a seamless way to unsubscribe from any sender directly from the summary. You can terminate unwanted connections instantly without the need to visit your management console.

searchDocs.title: Email Summary Contents​
searchDocs.content: An Email Summary consists of three primary sections: Sender Details, Email Alerts, and Action Shortcuts.  Sample Email Summary

searchDocs.title: Sender Details​
searchDocs.content: This section provides a brief overview of the source of the message:  Sender Name: The name associated with the sender's email account.Sender Email: The original email of the sender.Email Entrance: The specific Channel or Route address that received the email.

searchDocs.title: Email Alerts​
searchDocs.content: Alerts are displayed only when "invisible" or potentially risky elements are detected:  Tracked: The email contains tracking pixels designed to monitor when you open the message.Insecure Link: The email contains URLs that do not use the secure https protocol.Insecure Domains: When insecure links are detected, the system lists the specific domains associated with them for your review.Public Email Service: The sender's email address belongs to a public email service (such as Gmail, Yahoo, or Outlook). Be cautious if the sender claims to represent a business, since anyone can create an address with these providers.

searchDocs.title: Action Shortcuts​
searchDocs.content: Action Shortcuts are one-click links that allow you to instantly update how the system handles future emails from this sender. The available shortcuts vary based on the Route Type:  Allow Next: Permits exactly one additional email from this sender.Allow Future: Whitelists the sender to allow all future emails.Stop receiving email from domain: Silently blocks all future emails from the sender’s (exact) domain.Stop receiving email from email: Silently blocks all future emails from this specific email address.  Stop Receiving from a Domain on One Shot Routes​  A One Shot route lets each new sender through once, then blocks that exact address. Some senders use a different address for every email (for example bounce-code1@news.example.com, bounce-code2@news.example.com), so each one looks new and keeps getting through.  On emails that arrive through a One Shot route, the summary offers Stop receiving email from domain for the sender's domain. After you click it, every later email from that exact domain (in this example news.example.com) is blocked on that route, whatever address it comes from. Other domains, including subdomains and parent domains, are not affected.

searchDocs.title: Reply-All Warning​
searchDocs.content: When an email arriving at a channel's main address was also sent to other people, and some of them aren't contacts of that channel, the summary shows a red Warning row listing them. If you reply all, their replies to you are blocked until you add them as contacts. See Reply All on Received Emails.

searchDocs.title: The Sender in Your Inbox​
searchDocs.content: Every email Duotail delivers to you comes from your masked route or channel address, so your mail app can't show the real sender in the From field on its own. To help, the display name of the From field shows the original sender, for example:  Harry Potter harry3432.._at_gmail.com <1_a_happy.rhino_news@duotail.com>   The sender's address is written with _at_ instead of @. A long name before the @ is shortened with ..; the domain is always shown in full. The full address is in the Sender Email row of the summary.A long display name is shortened to 40 characters.Look-alike characters and invisible characters are removed from the name, so a sender can't pretend to be someone else.

searchDocs.title: Sender Verification​
searchDocs.content: Duotail delivers an incoming email only when the domain in its From field is verified by the email authentication standards (DMARC alignment, using SPF or DKIM). An email whose From address can't be verified, such as one with a forged sender, is deleted and never reaches you. This means the sender shown in the summary and in your inbox is one we can vouch for.  Emails forwarded by another mail server still arrive when the original sender's DKIM signature is intact, even though the forwarding server is not the sender's own.

searchDocs.title: Emails Without a Summary​
searchDocs.content: Some emails are delivered exactly as they were sent, with no summary table:  Encrypted-mail providers: Emails from senders at encrypted-mail providers such as Proton (proton.me, pm.me, protonmail.com, protonmail.ch) may be signed or encrypted. Changing their content would break the signature, so Duotail only replaces the headers needed to deliver them. These emails can't be scanned for tracking or insecure links, have no action shortcuts, and support replying to the sender only (no reply all). The sender is still shown in the From display name as described above.

searchDocs.title: What is a Route?​
searchDocs.content: A Route defines the rules for incoming emails. The text following the last underscore in an address is the Route ID. For example, in a_happy.rhino_food@duotail.com, food is the route. If a route rule allows deliciousgrass.com, any emails from that domain will be delivered to your inbox.

searchDocs.title: Route Email​
searchDocs.content: A Route Email is an address structured as <channel_id>_<route_id>@duotail.com. For an incoming email to pass through a route, it must comply with either the specific rules of that route or the general rules of the channel to which it belongs.

searchDocs.title: 🛡️ Zero-Knowledge Message Persistence​
searchDocs.content: We do not operate like a traditional, permanent email archive. Our gateway acts as a secure, zero-knowledge buffer:  Zero-Knowledge Persistence: We only persist processed emails in a zero-knowledge state using modern cryptographic primitives. Because we do not persist decryption keys, your messages are mathematically inaccessible to everyone — including us or any government entities.Dual-Action Purge Protocol: To minimize data liability, we provide two layers of deletion: On-Demand: You have the power to manually and permanently delete any encrypted record at any time via your dashboard.Automated: To ensure your digital footprint remains minimal, any message remaining in the buffer is automatically and permanently purged after 30 days. Irrecoverable Deletion: Once a purge is triggered—whether manually or automatically—the data is wiped from our active infrastructure and is completely unrecoverable.  For a full technical breakdown of our X25519, AES-256, and Argon2id implementation, please visit our Encryption Documentation.

searchDocs.title: 👤 Data Collection Practices​

searchDocs.title: 🔐 Technical Implementation​
searchDocs.content: Our protocol is divided into three distinct phases: Identity Generation, Message Protection, and Secure Retrieval.

searchDocs.title: Phase 1: Key Generation & Registration​
searchDocs.content: We use a public/private key architecture to ensure we never store the key that unlocks your emails.  User Entropy: The customer provides a unique combination of three words associated with a Key Name.Key Derivation: Our system applies the Argon2id hashing algorithm to your three words to derive a private key, then uses X25519 elliptic curve cryptography to compute its matching public key. The private key is discarded as soon as the public key is computed.Storage: Only the Key Name and the public key are stored in our secure database. A public key can only lock data; it cannot unlock it. Neither your three words nor your private key is ever persisted.

searchDocs.title: Phase 2: Message Protection (The Airlock)​
searchDocs.content: When an email enters our gateway, it is neutralized and secured before it touches our disk. 4. Encryption: Before the system saves any email content, it creates a one-time key pair for that email and combines it with your public key (X25519 key agreement) to produce a unique AES-256 key. The content is encrypted with that key in GCM mode, and the one-time private key is discarded. Only your private key, rebuilt from your three words, can recreate the AES key and decrypt the file. 5. Association: Once the encrypted .eml file is stored in our file system, we record which Key Name was used to secure it. This creates a link without exposing the content.

searchDocs.title: Phase 3: Secure Retrieval​
searchDocs.content: Retrieval is a "Just-in-Time" process. The decryption key exists only in memory for the duration of your request. 6. Challenge: When you request a download, our system retrieves the Key Name and prompts you for the associated three words. 7. Re-Generation: Using your provided words, the system re-runs the Argon2id process to reconstruct your private key (the Decryption Key). 8. Decryption & Delivery: The system loads the encrypted file, performs the decryption in a transient memory state, and streams the original file to you.

searchDocs.title: 🛡️ Why This Matters​
searchDocs.content: No Persistence of Secrets: Because we do not store your "three words," we have no way to reconstruct your decryption key.Mathematical Inaccessibility: Without your unique words, the stored .eml files are mathematically indistinguishable from random noise.Transient Memory: Decryption keys are generated on-the-fly and are never written to permanent storage.

searchDocs.title: ❓ Security FAQ​
searchDocs.content: What if I lose my three words? Because Duotail is a zero-knowledge system, we do not have a "backdoor" to your data. If you lose your three words, any messages already encrypted with that specific key become permanently inaccessible. We cannot reset the key for existing files because we never held the secret to begin with. Can I change my encryption settings?Yes. You maintain full control over your security configuration via your Account Page. You can update your encryption key at any time by providing a new Key Name and a new set of Three Words. Future Emails: All incoming emails received after the update will be secured using your new credentials.Legacy Emails: Messages previously encrypted will still require the original words used at the time of their arrival. What algorithms do you use? We rely on industry-standard primitives: AES-256 in GCM mode for data at rest, Argon2id for key derivation, and X25519 for key agreement.

searchDocs.title: Permissions​
searchDocs.content: Whether an incoming email is delivered to a user is determined by a combination of three types of permissions at the route level:  Domain Permission: This permission applies to a specific domain and all its subdomains. It can be set to either Enabled or Disabled. For example, if deliciousgrass.com is enabled, emails from both deliciousgrass.com and em.deliciousgrass.com are permitted.Email Permission: This permission applies to a specific email address. It can be either Enabled or Disabled. For example, if spmail@em.deliciousgrass.com is disabled, all emails from that specific address will be blocked.Stamp List: Any email addresses included in the Stamp List are automatically blocked.  Reply Handling If you reply to any email received through a route, an Email Permission for that sender will be automatically added to the route settings. This ensures that their future messages are always permitted.

searchDocs.title: Route Type​
searchDocs.content: There are two types of routes available for our users: subscription route and one-shot route.

searchDocs.title: Subscription Route​
searchDocs.content: A Subscription Route is designed to help users manage their email subscriptions effectively. It allows for the creation of comprehensive rules to tailor incoming email permissions specifically for subscription scenarios. Subscription route allows only Domain Permission and Email Permission.  First Email Auto Permission​  When a new Subscription Route is created, we recommend leaving the permissions undefined initially. If no permissions are set, the first email to reach the route will be automatically permitted. Furthermore, both the host domain of that email and its root domain will be added to your permission list with the status set to "Enabled." This feature is specifically designed to ensure that third-party confirmation emails reach your inbox without delay.  Subscription Route Incoming Email Decision Hierarchy​  When multiple permissions are set within a subscription route for emails from the same domain, the final decision is determined by a hierarchical "top-down" logic. The system searches for the most specific match first, moving to more general rules only if a match isn't found.  The Decision Hierarchy  Exact Email Match: The system first checks if the specific email address is listed. If a match is found, the email is Allowed or Denied based on that specific setting. Full Domain Match: If there is no specific email match, the system checks for a rule matching the exact domain (e.g., example.com). If a rule exists, it is applied immediately. Ancestor Domain Match: If no full domain match exists, the system looks for the closest ancestor domain (e.g., if the email is from sub.example.com, it looks for a rule for example.com). Final Fallback: If no matches are found at any level, the email is Denied by default.    Disabled Subcription Route​  If a subscription route is set to Disabled, any incoming emails directed to that specific route address are automatically trashed.

searchDocs.title: One-Shot Route​
searchDocs.content: A One-Shot Route is designed to handle "serendipity" style interactions, such as those originating from networking events or public inquiries. Under this route, only the first email from a new sender is delivered to your inbox.  In addition to standard domain and email permissions, the One-Shot Route utilizes a built-in Stamp List to track previous senders. Once a sender has messaged you, they are added to this list and subsequent emails from them are blocked. To allow a follow-up email from a specific sender, you can simply remove their address from the Stamp List.  Example: Suppose hug is a One-Shot Route under the channel a_happy.rhino.  If a new sender, angry.gazelle@example.com, sends an email to this route, the message will be delivered. However, any subsequent emails from angry.gazelle@example.com will be automatically discarded.  One-Shot Route Incoming Email Decision Hierarchy​  A One-Shot Route determines whether an email is delivered using the following hierarchy:  Permission Check: The system first follows the same decision hierarchy as a Subscription Route, checking all domain and email-level permissions. If an explicit "Enabled" permission is found, the email is delivered immediately. Stamp List Check: If no explicit permission is found in Step 1, the system checks the Stamp List. The email will be delivered only if the sender’s address is not already present on the list.  Disabled One-Shot Route​  If a One-Shot route is set to Disabled, any incoming emails directed to that specific route address are automatically trashed.  Locked One-Shot Route​  To protect against the risk of a One-Shot email address being leaked or falling into the wrong hands, these routes can be Locked.  When a route is locked, the system skips the Stamp List check and performs a Permission Check only. In this state, only emails from senders with explicit Enabled permissions will be delivered; all other incoming emails will be blocked.

searchDocs.title: Update Encryption Words​
searchDocs.content: You can rotate your encryption credentials at any time. This is a powerful security feature that ensures your future communications are protected by fresh keys.  How to Update​  Click the "Update Encryption Words" button.A window will appear with two sections: Key Name and File Encryption Words. Fill in your new details and click Save. If you are unsure what a field is for, hover over or click the ? icon next to its label for a short explanation.  Understanding the Form Fields​  If you are new to zero-knowledge encryption, here is exactly what these fields do:  Key Name Think of this as a public label for your secret words. What it does: It helps you remember which set of words you are currently using. If you have multiple keys over time, this label tells you which one to use when downloading a specific email.Rules: Maximum 8 characters. Use only letters and numbers (e.g., key2026, youguess). It's case insensitive.File Encryption Words These are your private master keys. What it does: Our system takes these three words and uses them as the "ingredient" to mathematically build a lock for your emails. Our Privacy Promise: We never store these words. They exist only in your mind or your password manager. Rules: Each word must be 12 characters or fewer. You can use letters, numbers, and special characters (like !@#$). These are case-sensitive (e.g., "Apple" is different from "apple").  The "Future-Only" Rule When you update your encryption words, the following happens: New Emails: All emails arriving after the update will be locked with your new words.Old Emails: Any emails currently in your buffer were locked with your previous words. To download them, you will still need to provide the words associated with the old Key Name.    🛠️ Technical Transparency​  Curious about the math? For a full technical breakdown of how we use Argon2id and X25519 to turn your three words into a zero-knowledge lock, visit our Data Encryption Protocol page.

Note: If you haven't whitelisted duotail.com in your inbox, the confirmation email may be in your spam/junk folder.

searchDocs.title: Related Topics​
searchDocs.content: You may also want to check out the following related topics  Alias Channel Whitelist Our Domain

searchDocs.title: A Tour of the Dashboard​
searchDocs.content: From top to bottom, the dashboard shows:  Area	What it is forNotices	Short messages about what just happened, such as a new email address being ready. Most can be closed with the × on the right. Action buttons	Create Email Address, Allow Incoming Emails and Add Inbox. Hover over a button to see a short tip. Activity → Listening Now	Email addresses that are temporarily open to a new sender. Only shown while at least one is open. Activity → Recent Emails	Your five latest emails and what happened to each one. View all in History opens the full list. Inboxes	Your inboxes. Each one has a main email address and a recipient, which is your own email address where Duotail delivers your mail. Send Pending	Emails you wrote that are waiting for you before they can go out. Only shown on a paid plan, and only when something is waiting.  What a free account can do A free account can receive emails and reply to them. Starting a new email and adding more inboxes require a paid plan. On a free account the Add Inbox button and the Send Pending section are not shown, and a notice with an Upgrade link appears at the top of the dashboard.

searchDocs.title: Two Words You Will See Often​
searchDocs.content: Inbox – a group of email addresses that all start with the same name. For example, the inbox a_happy.rhino owns a_happy.rhino@duotail.com (its main email) and every address that starts with a_happy.rhino_. Other pages of this documentation call an inbox a channel.Email address – an extra address inside an inbox that you create for one purpose, such as a_happy.rhino_news@duotail.com. Other pages call this a route.  Duotail does not store a mailbox for you to open. Email that is allowed through is forwarded to the recipient address of the inbox, so you keep reading and writing email in the mail app you already use.

searchDocs.title: Before You Start: Check Your Inbox Is Ready​
searchDocs.content: Look at the Inboxes table. An inbox can be used when its row shows a Manage button. If you see another button instead, click it first:  Activate – your own email address is not confirmed yet. Follow the confirmation link we emailed you.Initialize – the inbox needs a one-time setup. One click completes it.  Until this is done, a yellow notice above the table tells you which inboxes cannot receive email yet.

searchDocs.title: 1. Create an Email Address​
searchDocs.content: There are two ways to get a new email address. Use the first for everyday needs; use the second when you want a whole new inbox with its own main email.

searchDocs.title: Option A: Create Email Address​
searchDocs.content: Use this when you need an address to give out, for example when signing up for a website or a newsletter.  Click Create Email Address. The New Email Address window opens. Address – type a short name for the address, such as news. You can use lowercase letters, numbers and periods, up to 20 characters. The full address is shown as you type, for example a_happy.rhino_news@duotail.com. If you have more than one inbox, first choose which inbox the address belongs to. Delivery – choose which of your own email addresses should receive the mail. This step only appears if you have more than one confirmed email address. Purpose – choose how strict the address should be: Permission Enforced – best for subscriptions, online shopping, or membership sign-ups. The first email that arrives is let through and its sender is remembered; other senders are blocked until you allow them.Cold Reach Allowed – lets one email through from each person you have not heard from before. Use it for an address you hand out to people, such as on a business card. Details – describe what you will use the address for (up to 30 characters). For a Permission Enforced address you can also note who you expect to hear from. Confirm – check the summary and click Finish.  A green notice confirms that your new address is ready. Click Copy email address in the notice to copy it, then paste it wherever you need it.    tip You can create as many addresses as you like. Still, you do not need a new one for every website. We recommend keeping one address per purpose, such as one for all your newsletters and another for online shopping, and reusing it for every sender of that kind. Each time you give the address to a new sender, use Allow Incoming Emails to let that sender in.

searchDocs.title: Option B: Add Inbox (Paid Feature)​
searchDocs.content: Use this when you want a separate inbox with its own main email address, for example to keep work and personal email apart.  Click Add Inbox. The button is shown on a paid plan once you have a confirmed email address. Email – choose which of your own email addresses receives the mail for this inbox. Channel – type the name of the inbox. It must be 5–30 characters, using lowercase letters, numbers and dots, and it cannot start or end with a dot. The name is prefixed with a_, so happy.rhino becomes a_happy.rhino@duotail.com. Identity Channel – if this checkbox is shown, tick it to create an address without the a_ prefix. See Identity Channel for what this means. Click Submit.  Channel limits The Basic plan includes up to 3 alias inboxes (including the one created when you registered) and 1 identity inbox. When you have used all of one kind, the window says so, for example You've reached your plan's identity channel limit (1)., and only offers the kind you can still add. See Channel Limits by Plan.  The new inbox appears in the Inboxes table. If its row shows Initialize, click it to finish the setup. Use Copy Email on the row to copy the main email address.  note Only your contacts can send email to an inbox's main email address. To let someone reach it, create a contact for them.

searchDocs.title: 2. Receive Email​
searchDocs.content: Duotail blocks email by default and lets through only what you have allowed. There are three ways to allow a sender. Whichever you choose, the email is delivered to your recipient address and listed under Recent Emails.  You want to…	UseAlways receive email from a person you trust, on any address of an inbox	Create a contact Decide exactly which senders an email address accepts	Configure the email address Let one new sender through for a short time, such as a sign-up confirmation	Allow Incoming Emails

searchDocs.title: Option A: Create a Contact​
searchDocs.content: A contact is a sender you trust. Email from a contact always reaches the inbox's main email and every other address in that inbox.  In the Inboxes section, click Create a contact in the blue notice above the table. The Create Contact window opens. Who is this? – fill in: Email to Send – a short name of your choice. It becomes the address you write to when you want to email this contact, in the form 2_<name>@duotail.com.External Email – the contact's real email address.Name – a name to recognize the contact by (5–30 characters). Click Next. Where does it live? – choose the inbox (Channel) the contact belongs to. Route and Notes are optional. Click Finish. A short message confirms that the contact was created.  If you have closed the blue notice, reload the page to bring it back, or click Manage on the inbox and add the contact from its Contacts section. See Manage Contacts for viewing, changing and deleting contacts.

searchDocs.title: Option B: Configure the Email Address​
searchDocs.content: Every email address you create has its own list of permitted senders. You can edit that list at any time.  In the Inboxes table, click Manage on the inbox that owns the address.Find the address in the table and open it for editing.Add the sender's domain (for example example.com) or exact email address to its permissions and save.  The full walkthrough, including how to block a sender again, is in Manage Routes.  tip A new Permission Enforced address needs no configuration for its first sender. The first email that arrives is let through and that sender's domain is permitted from then on.

searchDocs.title: Option C: Allow Incoming Emails​
searchDocs.content: Use this when you are about to give an existing address to a new sender and expect an email soon, for example a confirmation email after signing up on another website.  Click Allow Incoming Emails. The Turn On Listening window opens. Which address should we watch? – choose the address the email will be sent to. If you have more than one inbox, choose the inbox first. How soon do you expect it? – choose 30 minutes, 1 hour or 8 hours. You can also note who the email is from. Check the summary and click Finish.  A yellow notice confirms that we are listening, and the address appears under Activity → Listening Now. From there you can Copy Email to paste the address into the other website, or Turn Off to stop early.  The next email from a new sender to that address is delivered, and that sender is permitted from then on. Listening then stops by itself. It also stops when the time you chose runs out.  Choose the shortest time Pick the shortest time in which you expect the email. The shorter the window, the less chance an unwanted sender gets through.  Good to know:  Only Permission Enforced addresses that already have at least one permitted sender are listed. A brand-new address does not need this step because it already accepts its first sender.Each inbox can listen on one address at a time. Turning on a new one replaces the current one; you are warned before this happens.If the window says you need an address first, create one and choose Permission Enforced.

searchDocs.title: 3. Send Email (Paid Feature)​
searchDocs.content: info Starting a new email requires a paid plan. On a free plan you can still reply to any email you received through Duotail.  You send email from your own mail app, not from the dashboard. Instead of writing to a person's real address, you write to their Duotail contact address, which starts with 2_. Duotail then delivers your email to the real address and shows your Duotail address as the sender, so your own email address stays private.  Always send from the recipient email address of the inbox. Email sent from any other address is not delivered.

searchDocs.title: Option A: Send to an Existing Contact​
searchDocs.content: Find the contact's Email to Send address. Click Manage on the inbox, then open its Contacts section. The address looks like 2_matt.kansher@duotail.com.In your own mail app, write a new email to that address and send it.  The email appears under Recent Emails with the status Sent.

searchDocs.title: Option B: Send First, Add the Contact Later​
searchDocs.content: You do not have to create a contact before writing. Make up a 2_ address on the spot and Duotail holds your email until you tell it who the address belongs to.  In your own mail app, write an email to a new address of the form 2_<name>@duotail.com, for example 2_matt.kansher@duotail.com, and send it. Open the dashboard. The email is listed in the Send Pending section. Click Send on its row. The Create Contact window opens with the Duotail Contact Address already filled in. Enter the contact's External Email (their real address) and a Name, then click Next. Choose the inbox the contact belongs to and click Finish. If you are asked for your File Encryption Words, enter your three encryption words. See Understanding Encryption Fields if you are unsure what these are.  The email leaves the Send Pending list and is sent. A notice asks you to check the History page for its final status. From now on, emails to that 2_ address are sent straight away, as in Option A.  The other buttons on a pending row:  View – read the email before deciding.Delete – discard the email without sending it.  Monthly sending limit Your plan includes a monthly number of emails you can send this way. Each recipient counts as one email. If you have reached the limit, a notice tells you so when you click Send, and the email stays in Send Pending until the limit resets next month.

searchDocs.title: Sending to Several People at Once​
searchDocs.content: You can put several 2_ addresses in To, Cc and Bcc of the same email. Everyone receives it from your Duotail address, and people in To and Cc can reply all. If some of the addresses don't have a contact yet, the email waits in Send Pending and Send walks you through creating each missing contact. See Sending to Several Contacts for the details.  When you receive an email that was also sent to other people, you can use Reply All in your mail app. See Reply All on Received Emails.

searchDocs.title: Where to Go Next​
searchDocs.content: Manage Routes – fine-tune who can reach each email address.Manage Contacts – view, change and delete contacts.Manage History – see every email and download or delete it.Manage Account – your profile, email addresses, encryption words and subscription.White List Our Domain – make sure emails from Duotail are not treated as junk.

searchDocs.title: How It Works​
searchDocs.content: Get your own Duotail inbox. When you sign up, you get an inbox with an address such as a_happy.rhino@duotail.com.Create an address for each purpose. Make one for shopping (a_happy.rhino_shopping@duotail.com), one for newsletters (a_happy.rhino_news@duotail.com), and so on. Give these out instead of your real address.Keep reading email where you already do. Emails you allow are forwarded to your own email address, such as your Gmail or Outlook, so you don't need to check a new mailbox every day. If you want to look back, the History page on our website lists your emails from the past 30 days, and you can open or download the ones we have kept for you.

searchDocs.title: What Makes Duotail Different​
searchDocs.content: Addresses that make sense. No random strings to copy and forget. You name each address after what it is for, like a_happy.rhino_shopping@duotail.com, so every email tells you at a glance who sent it and why.A "don't email me, I'll email you" main address. Your inbox's main address only accepts your contacts, the people you have chosen to trust. Anyone else is turned away, so it never fills up with strangers.Scam-resistant by default. Strangers can't reach you unless you let them, which shuts out most scam and phishing emails before they arrive. For the emails that do get through, the summary points out warning signs such as tracking pixels, insecure links, or a "business" writing from a free Gmail or Outlook address.Two kinds of addresses for two kinds of senders. A Permission Enforced address only accepts senders you have allowed, which is perfect for shopping and newsletters. A Cold Reach Allowed address lets each new person introduce themselves once, then waits for you to decide, which is ideal for a business card.Listen when you are expecting mail. About to sign up somewhere new? Open an address for a short time, and the next sender is let in and remembered. Then it closes again by itself.One click from every email. Each email we forward comes with a short summary and action links: allow the next email, allow this sender for good, or stop hearing from them. No settings page needed.Mute and unmute any time. Turn any sender off when they get noisy and back on when you want them again. Your inbox only gets the mail you actually want, so it stays lean instead of growing out of control.Your stored emails are locked. Emails we keep for you are encrypted with three secret words that only you know. See Data Security to learn more.

searchDocs.title: Get Started​
searchDocs.content: Signing up is free. A free account lets you create addresses, choose who can reach you, and reply to the emails you receive. When you register, your inbox is named after your username. For example, the username happy.rhino gets the inbox a_happy.rhino.  Keep our emails out of your junk folder Duotail is a new service, so some email providers may not recognize us yet. Before you register, add duotail.com to your safe senders list so you receive your confirmation email and forwarded mail: Gmail · Outlook  Register a free accountFollow the Quick Start guide to create your first address and receive your first email.  You don't have to set everything up in advance When you create an address for shopping or newsletters, choose Permission Enforced. A new address of this kind lets the first sender through automatically and remembers it. Just sign up on the website, and its emails will keep arriving from then on.

searchDocs.title: Words You Will See​
searchDocs.content: You only need to know a few terms. The website and this documentation sometimes use different names for the same thing, so both are listed below.  Name on the website	Also called	What it meansInbox	Channel	Your group of Duotail addresses. They all start with the same name, such as a_happy.rhino. Email address	Route	One address inside your inbox, made for one purpose, such as a_happy.rhino_shopping@duotail.com. Each one keeps its own list of allowed senders. Contact	Contact	A person you trust. Their emails reach every address in your inbox, without any extra setup. Permission A sender you have allowed (or blocked) on an address. It can be a whole website, such as example.com, or a single email address.

searchDocs.title: Need Help?​
searchDocs.content: We are happy to help with any problem or question.  Help using Duotail: support@duotail.comAnything else: contact@duotail.com

searchDocs.title: How to Ensure Duotail Emails Reach Your Inbox
Why is this necessary?​
searchDocs.pageTitle: How to Ensure Duotail Emails Reach Your Inbox
searchDocs.content: Our service is in its early stages, and major providers are still learning to recognize our domain. Without whitelist our domain, your emails through our service will be sent to junk/spam folder. By setting this filter, you are telling your provider that you trust duotail.com, which helps us improve our reputation and ensures your emails reach your inbox as intended.

searchDocs.title: Whitelist in Gmail​
searchDocs.pageTitle: How to Ensure Duotail Emails Reach Your Inbox

searchDocs.title: Option 1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: How to Ensure Duotail Emails Reach Your Inbox
searchDocs.content: Step 1: Log into your Gmail account on a browser and type from:(duotail.com) in the top search bar then click show search options icon.    Step 2: Click Create filter link at the right bottom of the dropdown window.    Step 3: Check option Never send it to Spam then click Create filter button at the bottom. As optional, you can set Categorize as: Primary.

searchDocs.title: Option 2​
searchDocs.pageTitle: How to Ensure Duotail Emails Reach Your Inbox
searchDocs.content: Step 1: Log in to your Gmail account and click the Settings (gear icon) in the top right corner, then select See all settings.  Step 2: Navigate to Filters Click on the Filters and Blocked Addresses tab at the top of the menu.  Step 3: Create a New Filter Scroll down and click on Create a new filter.  Step 4: Enter the Domain in the From field, type: duotail.com  Step 5: Click Create filter at the bottom of the window. Step 2: Select Mail > Junk email in the popup window  Step 3: Click Add safe sender button from the Safe senders and domains tab  Step 4: Type duotail.com in the text box and click OK button  Step 5: Click Save button to save the change.

searchDocs.title: Summary​
searchDocs.content: Route Management is located within the Channel section of each individual channel page. In addition to managing specific routes, this section includes a Channel Settings segment at its top. Here, users can view or update global channel configurations, which serve as the default values for every new route created within that channel.  To access the Route Management section, simply click the Manage or Initialize button for any channel listed on your Home Page.

searchDocs.title: Route Table​
searchDocs.content: The Route Table is the central component of the Channel section, displaying all existing routes configured under the current channel. Each row in the table provides a summary of a specific route's configuration:  Route ID: The unique identifier for the route.Description: A user-defined label or note describing the route's purpose.Recipient: The destination email address where messages passing through this route are delivered.Type: The specific classification of the route - Subscription or One Shot.Status: The current state of the route - Enabled, Disabled, or Locked.Actions: Management tools available for the route.

searchDocs.title: Update Default Channel Settings​
searchDocs.content: You can modify your default configurations by clicking the Edit Channel Settings button. The following settings are available in the configuration window:  Channel Name: The unique identifier for the current channel. This is a read-only field.Sender Name: The default name displayed on all outgoing emails sent through this channel. If this field is left empty (the default state upon initialization), the system will use your name when registered.Channel Email: A dropdown menu that allows you to change the channel's destination to any verified email address associated with your account.  Security Note We actively monitor sender names for compliance. To prevent phishing and fraud, any attempt to misguide recipients by using a deceptive sender name will result in immediate account suspension.

searchDocs.title: Create Routes​
searchDocs.content: You can create a route by clicking the Add Route button located below the bottom of the Route Table. The Add Route configuration window features two tabs: Essential and Permissions.

searchDocs.title: Route Essentails​
searchDocs.content: The Essential tab contains the primary fields required to create a route:  Route ID: A unique identifier for the new route.Description: A brief note explaining the purpose of the route.Recipient: A dropdown menu to select the destination email address where messages received via this route will be delivered.Type: A dropdown menu to select the route logic—either Subscription or One Shot.Expected Sender (Optional): A friendly name (up to 20 characters) for the sender you expect to hear from first, such as Netflix. This field appears only for Subscription routes. When the first email arrives on a route with no permissions, the system automatically creates domain permissions for that sender and uses this value as their name. If you leave it empty, the sender's root domain (e.g., example.com) is used as the name instead. The field is disabled once the route has any permissions; in that case, set the Expected Sender through a Route Listener.

searchDocs.title: Route Permissions​
searchDocs.content: The Permissions tab lets you set access rules for the route. Each rule is either a Domain permission (e.g., example.com) or an Email permission (a full email address). Rules are shown in permission groups, one group per sender name, so you can manage all the domains and addresses of one sender together.  Changes Apply on Save Changes you make on the Permissions tab, including adding, toggling, editing, renaming and deleting, take effect only after you click Save. If you close the window without saving, they are discarded.  Add a Permission​  To add a new rule, fill in the fields at the bottom of the tab and click the + button:  Name (Optional): The sender name the permission belongs to (up to 20 characters). It decides which group the permission joins. If left empty, the value itself is used as the group name.Value: The specific domain (e.g., example.com) or the full email address you wish to manage.Type: A dropdown menu to specify whether the value is a Domain or an Email.  A newly added permission is always Enabled.  Permission Groups​  Permissions are grouped by their name. Every domain and email that shares exactly the same name appears in one group. Group names are case sensitive: Local News and local news are two separate groups.  Each group is shown in one of two ways:  Collapsed: A colored pill showing the group name and the number of permissions it contains. Click the pill to expand it.Expanded: A card with the group name in the header and one row per domain or email. Click the group name in the header to collapse it again.  The color of a collapsed pill, and of the toggle in an expanded group's header, shows the overall status of the group:  Green: All permissions in the group are enabled.Amber: Some permissions are enabled and some are disabled.Gray: All permissions in the group are disabled.  Manage Permissions​  Each permission has one of two statuses:  Enabled (Green Toggle): Emails from the specified domain or address are allowed through the route.Disabled (Gray Toggle): Emails from the specified domain or address are blocked.  In an expanded group, you can manage the whole group with the buttons in its header:  Toggle: Enables every permission in the group. If all of them are already enabled, it disables them all instead.Edit (pencil): Renames the group. All permissions in the group take the new name.Delete (trash can): Removes every permission in the group.  You can also manage individual permissions with the buttons on each row:  Toggle: Switches that permission between Enabled and Disabled.Edit (pencil): Changes the domain or email value. The new value must be a valid domain or email address of the same type.Delete (x): Removes that permission from the route.  To understand how our system decides whether an email is permitted when several permissions overlap, see our Route Guide for a detailed explanation of the decision hierarchy.  Group or Regroup Permissions​  Because groups are formed by name, you organize permissions by changing their names:  Merge groups: Rename a group to the exact name of another group (including letter case). All its permissions move into that group.Move a single permission: Add the same value and type again using the fields at the bottom of the tab, with the name of the target group. The existing permission is replaced, so it moves into that group. It is also set back to Enabled.Split a group: Move individual permissions out to a new name as described above.  Name Your Senders Auto-created permissions are named after the Expected Sender if you set one; otherwise they use the sender's root domain. Rename those groups to a friendly name, such as Safari News, to keep all of a sender's domains and addresses together.  Empty Permission Subscription We recommend leaving permissions undefined when creating a new Subscription route. If no explicit permissions are set, the system will automatically permit the first incoming email it receives. This is particularly useful for handling automated confirmation or verification emails generated by third-party services.

searchDocs.title: Update Routes​
searchDocs.content: You can update a route's configuration by clicking the Update button located in the Actions column of the Route Table.The Edit Route configuration window features the same two tabs—Essential and Permissions—for all route types.  Essential Tab: Allows you to update the route description, change the recipient email address, or modify the route status.Permissions Tab: Displays all existing access rules for the route. You can refine these rules to suit your needs; for detailed instructions, please refer to the Manage Permissions section.  If you are editing a One Shot route, an additional Blocked tab will appear. This allows you to manage the specific email addresses currently in the stamped list.

searchDocs.title: Manage Stamped List​
searchDocs.content: Every email address in the One Shot stamped list is displayed as a red pill within the Blocked tab. To remove an address from this list, simply click the x icon on the right side of the pill. Removing an address from the stamped list allows one additional email from that sender to pass through the route.The Blocked tab displays up to 30 email address pills at a time. If you cannot find a specific address, use the search bar at the top to filter the list by typing any part of the email address.

searchDocs.title: Delete Routes​
searchDocs.content: You can delete a route by clicking the Delete button located in the Actions column of the Route Table. A Delete Route confirmation window will appear, showing the full email address of the route.Click Delete to confirm, or Cancel to keep the route. Once a route is deleted:  New emails sent to the route's address will no longer be delivered.Replies to past emails received through this route will no longer reach the original sender. These replies are dropped silently: you will not receive a bounce or any other notice that your reply was not delivered.Email history for the route is kept and remains viewable.Route Listener: If the channel's active Route Listener is set on this route, it is turned off automatically. A listener on a different route is not affected.

searchDocs.title: Reusing a Deleted Route ID​
searchDocs.content: Once a route is deleted, its Route ID becomes available again, and you can create a new route with the same ID in the same channel. Because the Route ID is part of the route's email address, keep the following in mind:  The new route starts fresh. None of the old route's settings, such as its description, recipient or permissions, are restored.The new route uses the same email address as the deleted one, so senders who still have that address can reach you again, subject to the new route's permissions.Replies and action links in emails forwarded by the old route will apply to the new route.  warning Deleting a route takes effect immediately. If you only want to stop emails temporarily, consider changing the route's status to Disabled from the Update Routes window instead.

searchDocs.title: 👂 Route Listener​
searchDocs.content: A Route Listener is a temporary, high-intelligence state you can apply to your channel. It is designed to simplify the process of aggregating multiple subscriptions or new senders into a single route without manual whitelisting.

searchDocs.title: 🎯 Purpose​
searchDocs.content: The Route Listener allows you to bypass existing filters for a short window to capture a new connection.  Seamless Aggregation: Easily bring new subscription services into an existing route.Auto-Permissioning: Instead of manually configuring whitelists, the listener performs First Email Auto-Permission - automatically whitelisting the domain of the next incoming email.

searchDocs.title: ⚙️ How it Works​
searchDocs.content: When a Route Listener is active on a specific Route ID:  It temporarily ignores existing permission blocks for that route.It waits for the next incoming email.Once an email arrives, the gateway automatically whitelists the sender's domain.The listener then self-destructs, returning the route to its standard, secure state.

searchDocs.title: ⏳ Lifecycle & Limitations​
searchDocs.content: The Lifecycle​  A Route Listener remains active until one of the following occurs:  Successful Capture: An email is processed and the domain is whitelisted.Expiration: The user-defined "Active Duration" is reached.Manual Cancellation: The user stops the listener via the dashboard.  Key Constraints​  Subscription Routes with Permissions Only: Listeners can only be added to existing, Enabled routes of the "Subscription" type that already have at least one permission. A subscription route with no permissions doesn't need a listener: it automatically permits the first incoming email, using the route's own Expected Sender to name the new permissions.Single Instance: To prevent gateway conflicts, each channel can only have one active Route Listener at a time. Activating a new listener will automatically cancel any previous one on that channel.Visibility: The "Add Route Listener" button only appears if your channel has at least one enabled subscription route with at least one permission.

searchDocs.title: 🛠 Instructions​
searchDocs.content: Adding a Route Listener​  Click the "Add Route Listener" button above your route table.Configure the listener through the "Add Route Listener" form which contains the following options and Save Route ID: Select the specific route you wish to open for auto-permissioning.Active Duration: Select a lifespan from the dropdown: 30 minutes, 1 hour, or 8 hours.Expected Sender (Optional): A friendly name (up to 20 characters) for the sender you expect to hear from, such as Netflix. When the next email arrives, the domain permissions created for its sender use this value as their name, so they appear under that name in the route's permission groups. If you leave it empty, the sender's root domain (e.g., example.com) is used as the name instead. To add the new sender to an existing group, enter that group's name exactly as it appears; names are case sensitive.  Security Recommendation Always choose the shortest timeframe in which you expect the next email to arrive. This minimizes the "open window" for your route.    Removing a Route Listener​  If a listener is active, a yellow notification banner will appear at the top of your Route table.  To stop the listener manually, click the "Turn Off" button located on the right side of the banner.  The "Just-in-Time" Workflow The Route Listener is perfect for signing up for new services or newsletters. The Workflow: Select 30 minutes, hit Save, and then immediately submit your email address on the third-party website.Why it’s better: By choosing the shortest duration, you ensure that once the confirmation email arrives and the domain is whitelisted, the "airlock" closes immediately, keeping your route secure against any other potential noise.
